strategic_context: Middle East risk is evolving from a single Hormuz chokepoint into a multi-node energy resilience test; Brent remaining below $100 suggests inventories, alternative routes and non-OPEC supply are still functioning as shock absorbers.

brief.title: Energy Shock
brief.summary: Risk is expanding from Hormuz into Saudi energy infrastructure and Bab el-Mandeb, turning a single-chokepoint disruption into a broader multi-node energy-system shock.

brief.title: Saudi Infrastructure
brief.summary: Alternative supply infrastructure is itself becoming exposed, reducing the effective redundancy available when primary Gulf routes are disrupted.

brief.title: Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb
brief.summary: Alternative routes provide resilience only when their accessibility and failure risks remain sufficiently independent from the primary route.

brief.title: Oil Resilience
brief.summary: Brent remaining below $100 despite severe regional disruption suggests inventories, alternative routing, non-OPEC supply and demand adaptation are absorbing part of the shock.

brief.title: Strategic Option Value
brief.summary: Effective resilience depends on capacity, accessibility during stress and failure independence—not simply on the number of available alternatives.

brief.title: Fed Transmission
brief.summary: Higher oil prices are renewing inflation pressure and pushing Treasury yields higher, narrowing the Fed's policy flexibility and increasing equity discount-rate pressure.

brief.title: Rates / FX Divergence
brief.summary: The combination of higher U.S. Treasury yields and a weaker dollar warrants monitoring whether rising yields increasingly reflect inflation, fiscal or risk premia rather than stronger U.S. growth.

brief.title: Commodity CapEx Cycle
brief.summary: Oil and copper strength represent distinct inflation channels: geopolitical supply disruption versus investment-demand pressure from infrastructure and capital formation.
